title: The Screen Behind the Audition
text:
Until the 1970s the top American symphony orchestras were almost entirely male, and their music directors had great personal discretion over who was hired. Starting in the 1970s and 1980s, many orchestras changed their audition rules. Candidates played behind a screen so that the jury could hear but not see them. Some orchestras even laid down a carpet so that the sound of footsteps would not reveal whether a candidate was wearing heels.

The economists Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse wanted to know whether the screens had made a difference. They gathered audition records from several major orchestras, along with the orchestras' membership rosters over many years. Because some candidates auditioned both with and without screens at different times, they could compare how the same musicians fared under both systems.

Their estimates suggested that the screens increased the chance that a woman would advance from the early rounds of an audition and be hired in the end. They concluded that blind auditions could explain a meaningful share of the rise in the proportion of women in these orchestras, which grew from a small minority in 1970 to roughly a quarter by the mid 1990s.
lesson: If you want to judge people on their work alone, hide what should not matter. Simple changes to how you evaluate can remove biases you do not see in yourself.
source: Goldin, C., and Rouse, C. (2000). Orchestrating impartiality: The impact of 'blind' auditions on female musicians. American Economic Review, 90(4), 715-741.
caveat: Later critics pointed out that many of the paper's estimates are statistically imprecise, so the size of the effect is uncertain even though the principle is widely accepted.
